title: Ginzburg-Landau Theory with Elastic Incompatibility Describes the Liquid-G-phase-Crystal State Diagram
abstract: We derive a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory for the metastable heterogeneous G state reported in deeply undercooled metallic liquids. The central result is that type-II-like mixed-state physics can emerge structurally with the random internal stress field playing the role of the magnetic field. Frozen eigenstrain due to elastic incompatibility between ordered cores and the amorphous matrix generates incompatible stress, while the non-affine internal strain in the liquid-like matrix in between the ordered cores relaxes that stress over a finite screening length $λ_σ$ (analogous to the London length in the superconducting problem). Structural order heals over a distinct mechanically-dressed length $ξ_G$; their ratio $κ_G=λ_σ/ξ_G$ provides the structural counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter. Because the matrix is transiently rigid yet locally relaxational only over an intermediate time window, the same mechanism selects crystal for slow protocols, a heterogeneous G state at intermediate rates, and a homogeneous L-like glass under rapid arrest. Residual incompatibility frustrates coarsening, allowing finite ordered cores and screened, orientation-dependent core interactions. The resulting texture is an inverted Abrikosov analogue: structural order resides in the cores, whereas incompatible-stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory yields direct simulation and experimental tests through stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine-susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.
summary: This work develops a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory to explain the liquid-glass-crystal phase diagram in metallic liquids. It shows that the intermediate, heterogeneous G state emerges due to a structural analogue of type-II superconductivity, where incompatible internal stresses are screened by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory provides testable predictions linking structural healing lengths and stress screening lengths.
main_problem: To determine if a mechanism analogous to type-II superconductivity can arise in structural condensed matter systems, specifically in deeply undercooled metallic liquids.
main_result: The theory predicts a heterogeneous G state, analogous to a mixed superconducting state, where structural order resides in cores and stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix.
method: Derivation of a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory incorporating elastic incompatibility and non-affine internal strain.
model_or_system: The system is deeply undercooled metallic liquids undergoing a first-order transition between liquid (L), heterogeneous glassy (G), and crystalline (X) states. The model uses an order parameter $\phi(r)$ and incorporates structural mismatch ($\epsilon^*_{ij}$) and non-affine strain ($p_{ij}$).
key_observables: Stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.
important_parameters: Structural screening length ($\lambda_σ$), structural healing length ($\xi_G$), and the structural Ginzburg-Landau parameter ($\kappa_G = \lambda_σ/\xi_G$).
main_assumptions: The analogy to superconductivity is used as an organizing principle, and the theory relies on projecting the elastic strain onto a deviatoric channel to simplify the free energy functional.
figures_summary: Figure 2 illustrates the temperature–stress state diagram showing boundaries $\sigma_{c1}$ and $\sigma_{c2}$ defining the stability regions of the different phases.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by defining the free energy functional based on elastic incompatibility, deriving the mechanical equilibrium equations, and then projecting the problem onto a reduced, mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau form to predict the mixed-state texture.
why_interesting: The concept of using elastic incompatibility and stress screening mechanisms, analogous to superconducting physics, to describe structural phase transitions in disordered materials is a powerful, generalizable theoretical framework for understanding complex many-body dynamics.
